soil-fert-060.title: Calcium carbonate equivalent: rating a lime's strength
soil-fert-060.text: Some limestone outperforms pure calcium carbonate at its own job. Calcium carbonate equivalent, or CCE, compares a liming material's neutralizing power with that of pure calcium carbonate. Limestones containing dolomite can rate above 100 percent, because magnesium carbonate is lighter than calcium carbonate. Fineness matters too, since soil acids are weak. Particles over 8 mesh are of little value, 8–60 mesh somewhat effective, and anything finer than 60 mesh fully effective. The effective calcium carbonate equivalent (ECCE) combines CCE with fineness; commercial aglime typically ranges from 45 to 110 percent. Marl, with less calcium carbonate, is spread at rates adjusted by its CCE.

soil-fert-061.title: The lime that turned Brazil's cerrado into farmland
soil-fert-061.text: Before the 1960s, Brazil's inland cerrado was considered unfit for farming. Its soil was too acidic and too poor in nutrients. Then lime arrived on a vast scale. By the late 1990s Brazil was spreading 14–16 million tonnes a year, rising to 25 million tonnes in 2003 and 2004, about five tonnes per hectare. The result helped make Brazil the world's second-biggest soybean exporter.

soil-fert-080.title: Marling, one of farming's oldest soil fixes
soil-fert-080.text: In 18th-century Lancashire, almost every field had its marl pit. Marling, spreading marl or raw chalk and lime debris on fields, is one of the oldest soil amendments in agriculture. Britain used it sporadically from prehistoric times, and Pliny the Elder mentioned it in the 1st century. Wider use from the 16th century contributed to the early modern agricultural revolution. Early in the 19th century, lime and imported mineral fertilizers gradually replaced it. Yet by the late 19th century New Jersey was mining marl industrially, grading it and publishing detailed chemical analyses.

soil-fert-041.title: Night soil, the town's waste carted to the fields
soil-fert-041.text: Ancient Athens channeled its sewage to the Cephissus valley as fertilizer. In Edo, compost merchants sold feces to farmers, and Aztec chinampas were built of mud and human waste. Night soil is the old euphemism for such waste: human excreta collected, usually at night, from cesspools, privies, pail closets and pit latrines. It came from towns without sewers or septic systems, gathered undiluted by water, and was sometimes carted out of town and sold as fertilizer. Unprocessed, it is risky. Parasitic worm infections such as ascariasis are linked to its use, because the eggs pass from person to person in feces. Composting and other proper handling of fecal sludge reduce these risks.

soil-fert-042.title: Closing the loop: human excreta as fertilizer
soil-fert-042.text: In Africa, the nutrients theoretically recoverable from human excreta match all current fertilizer use. That makes excreta a possible alternative for smallholders, who often cannot afford chemical fertilizer. Reusing treated excreta for its nutrients, organic matter and energy 'closes the loop' between sanitation and farming, and it is central to ecological sanitation. The products differ: urine, dried feces, composted feces, fecal sludge, sewage and sewage sludge each fertilize in their own way. Treatments such as urine diversion and drying, composting, and sludge treatment remove pathogens to varying degrees and cut water content. The advantages are real. Fertilizers made from mined phosphate rock can carry cadmium and uranium into the food chain, but excreta-based ones generally lack these heavy metals. Their nutrients are bound in organic compounds or held on humic acids, so they release slowly and leach less readily than mineral fertilizers. Like other nitrogen fertilizers, though, they can let nitrate leach away. Pharmaceutical residues in excreta break down better in soil than in water. People have farmed with excreta for centuries, often in unregulated and unsafe ways in developing countries. Whether reuse is cost-effective is still debated.

soil-fert-037.title: Humanure, compost made from people
soil-fert-037.text: Organic farmer Joseph Jenkins coined the word humanure for human excreta used as a nutrient-rich composting input. In soil it builds organic matter and healthy microbial communities. Feces supply nitrogen, urine supplies phosphorus, and both are a good source of potassium. Feces can carry bacteria, viruses and parasitic worms, but proper fermentation kills pathogens and parasite eggs within two weeks to six months, depending on climate. Urine helps. Added to compost, it raises the temperature, helping destroy pathogens and seeds, and unlike feces it does not attract flies or carry worm eggs.

soil-fert-038.title: The composting toilet: sawdust instead of a flush
soil-fert-038.text: Most composting toilets use no flush water at all. They are dry toilets that treat human waste by composting it into a compost-like material. After each use, a carbon additive such as sawdust, {{ref:soil-agri-139}} or peat moss goes in. It makes air pockets, improves the C:N ratio and cuts odor. Most rely on mesophilic composting, at moderate temperatures. Long retention or a second composting step kills more pathogens and gives a humus-like product that can enrich soil where rules allow. Its nutrients are more available to plants than those in dried feces from urine-diverting dry toilets. Using it in one's own garden is regarded as safe, though because pathogens can survive, legal restrictions may apply.

soil-fert-045.title: Biosolids: sewage sludge returned to the land
soil-fert-045.text: Farmers began spreading sewage sludge in the 1920s. Treated, that sludge is called biosolids: solid organic matter recovered from sewage treatment and used as fertilizer or soil conditioner. Research confirms biosolids hold nutrients similar to those in animal manures. They can supply nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur and micronutrients, and they are 60–65% organic matter that stimulates soil microbes. They come as cake, granules, pellets or liquid, spread and worked into the soil or injected directly. Sludge has been shown to raise soil available phosphorus, and soil salt levels too. The trouble is what else rides along. Biosolids can contain synthetic organic compounds, radionuclides and heavy metals. {{ref:soil-env-200}} from spread biosolids have contaminated farm soils, groundwater, animals and crops. Heavy metals and persistent pharmaceutical pollutants make spreading sludge controversial in the USA and parts of Europe, and some places ban biosolids on farmland. One study found that high-temperature pyrolysis of biosolids into biochar reduced those chemicals below detectable limits.

soil-fert-043.title: Urine, the nitrogen-rich share of human waste
soil-fert-043.text: Urine makes up less than 1% of the volume of sewage, yet it carries about 70% of its nitrogen and more than half its potassium. As a crop fertilizer it is rich in nitrogen, mostly as urea, and in potassium. Design values are 4 kg nitrogen, 0.36 kg phosphorus and 1.0 kg potassium per person per year, about 7:1.5:2.2 as N:P2O5:K2O. The amounts vary with diet, and nitrogen rises with the protein eaten. Its fertilizing effect is comparable to commercial nitrogen fertilizers, and it holds far less lead, mercury and cadmium than sewage sludge. Undiluted urine can burn leaves or roots, especially in dry soil. So it is diluted, 1:5 for container crops or 1:8 for general use. Too much brings excess nitrogen and salts such as sodium chloride, and can cause excess ammonia, acidity or other harm to plants. In storage its urea quickly hydrolyzes to ammonia. Delivering it through perforated hoses about 10 cm below the surface cuts odor, ammonia loss and pathogen transfer. Health risks are generally regarded as negligible, especially when urine goes into the soil rather than onto edible plant parts.

soil-fert-044.title: Feces as fertilizer: nutrients plus carbon
soil-fert-044.text: By Swedish default values, an adult excretes 0.55 kg nitrogen, 0.18 kg phosphorus and 0.36 kg potassium in feces a year. That gives wet feces an NPK% of 1.1:0.8:0.9. Urine, by comparison, can hold up to 90% of the nitrogen, 50% of the phosphorus and 70% of the potassium in human excreta. Feces also add organic carbon. Post-treated dried feces from urine-diverting dry toilets raise harvests through their nutrients and improve soil fertility through that carbon. Fecal sludge from pit latrines, septic systems and dry toilets can be made fit for farm use by dewatering, drying, composting, pelletizing or anaerobic digestion.

soil-fert-047.title: The multiple barrier approach to safe reuse
soil-fert-047.text: Reusing excreta safely depends on a series of barriers rather than any single step. World Health Organization guidelines of 2006 on safe reuse of wastewater, excreta and greywater rest on this multiple barrier approach. Treatment is one barrier. Others include the choice of crop, farming and application methods, and farmer education. How much treatment is needed depends on which other barriers are in use. Temperatures above 50 °C, as in thermophilic composting or digestion, inactivate most pathogens. So does a pH above 10, from ammonia or lime treatment. Helminth eggs, the eggs of parasitic worms, are among the hardest pathogens to destroy, so reuse schemes use them as indicator organisms.

soil-fert-083.title: The salt index: how hard a fertilizer pulls on water
soil-fert-083.text: Potassium chloride has a salt index of 116.2. Urea scores 74.4, and diammonium phosphate 29.2. The fertilizer salt index measures how much a fertilizer raises the osmotic pressure of water, the pull dissolved salts exert, compared with sodium nitrate set at 100. Fertilizers with an index above 20 are not recommended for particularly sensitive crops. Using too much fertilizer, or one with too high an index, builds up salts in the soil and causes burns.

soil-fert-049.title: The microbes inside a biofertilizer
soil-fert-049.text: The longest-used biofertilizer organisms are nitrogen fixers: Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum and blue-green algae. Each suits different crops. Rhizobium inoculant serves legumes. Azotobacter goes to crops such as wheat, maize, cotton and potato, and Azospirillum mainly to sorghum, millets, maize, sugarcane and wheat. Blue-green algae such as Nostoc and Anabaena inoculate paddy crops. Anabaena paired with the water fern Azolla can add up to 60 kg/ha of nitrogen a season. Other organisms used include Bacillus and Bradyrhizobium bacteria, Trichoderma fungi and Gigaspora mycorrhizal fungi. In coastal districts, seaweeds rich in potassium, phosphorus and trace elements are widely used in place of manure.

soil-fert-202.title: Coated urea: a shell that slows the nitrogen
soil-fert-202.text: Coat a urea prill, a small bead of fertilizer, in something less soluble and its nitrogen seeps out slowly. Coated urea releases urea gradually, lowering the risk of fertilizer burn and allowing less frequent applications. Sulfur-coated urea, developed by the Tennessee Valley Authority, holds 32% to 41% nitrogen. It releases once water enters cracks in the coating; a wax seal slows it further until microbes degrade it. Polymer-coated urea releases nitrogen more precisely, with release delayable for 10 months, but it costs more. Combination products coat urea with sulfur and then polymer, a cheaper route to precise release.

soil-fert-085.title: Urease inhibitors: buying time for urea
soil-fert-085.text: Urea left on the soil surface can lose its nitrogen to the air. Urease inhibitors block the urease enzyme, so urea stays in its non-volatile form for longer. That gives rain time to carry the urea into the soil, where hydrolysis happens below the surface and less nitrogen escapes. The inhibitors also shrink the zones of high pH around untreated urea. Most studies find they reduce nitrogen losses when fertilizer must be applied in poor field conditions. They help most under high-residue {{ref:soil-agri-099}}.

soil-fert-013.title: Stabilized nitrogen: slowing fertilizer down in the soil
soil-fert-013.text: Nitrogen fertilizer works better when it changes form more slowly in the soil. Two kinds of additive slow it. Nitrification inhibitors, also called nitrogen stabilizers, suppress the biological oxidation of ammonia into nitrate, an anion more prone to leaching. Urease inhibitors such as NBPT, added to urea fertilizers at 0.05 weight percent, slow urea's enzymatic hydrolysis into ammonia, which can evaporate or be turned into nitrate. A fertilizer carrying such an additive is called stabilized: its nitrogen stays in the soil longer in urea or ammonium form. Using them lets farmers limit the polluting effects of nitrogen washing off their fields.

soil-fert-074.title: Landfill leachate, the liquid that seeps from waste
soil-fert-074.text: Rain falling on a landfill does not simply vanish. It percolates through the waste and emerges as landfill leachate, a contaminated liquid that can pollute groundwater if not managed. Its makeup varies with the landfill's age and waste type. It carries dissolved and suspended matter, and decomposition adds organic acids, aldehydes, alcohols and simple sugars. Siting landfills on impermeable ground, or lining them with geomembranes or engineered clay, cuts the risk; bentonite is used to line landfill bases. In a 2012 New York survey, all double-lined landfill cells leaked less than 500 liters per hectare per day. Granular laterite in purpose-built treatment beds has removed phosphorus and heavy metals from leachate.

soil-fert-008.title: Phosphate fertilizers, from rock to soluble salt
soil-fert-008.text: Each ton of phosphoric acid made from phosphate rock leaves five tons of phosphogypsum, an impure radioactive waste. The world produces 100 to 280 million tons of it a year. That waste is the shadow of phosphate fertilizers, which supply phosphorus from rock whose main minerals are fluorapatite and hydroxyapatite. Acid treatment turns those minerals into water-soluble phosphate salts, and this use is the main reason so much sulfuric acid is made. The main straight phosphate fertilizers are the acid-treated rock products of {{ref:soil-fert-094}}. The single kind has 14–18% P2O5 plus phosphogypsum; the triple kind has 44–48% P2O5 and no gypsum. A maize crop yielding 6–9 tonnes of grain per hectare needs 31–50 kg of phosphate fertilizer, and soybeans about half, 20–25 kg. Billions of kilograms of rock are mined each year, but the remaining ore is shrinking in size and quality, making future supply a critical issue. Phosphate also pollutes. Normally a limiting nutrient in water, at high concentrations it promotes cyanobacteria and algae, and it is the main contributor to {{ref:soil-env-020}}.

soil-fert-017.title: The cadmium, fluoride and uranium in some fertilizers
soil-fert-017.text: Monoammonium phosphate can hold anywhere from 0.14 to 50.9 mg/kg of cadmium, and phosphate rock up to 188 mg/kg. Some fertilizers, especially phosphate and slag-based ones, add such contaminants to soils: cadmium, fluoride, uranium and other heavy metals. Continued use of high-cadmium fertilizer can contaminate soils and plants, so producers now choose phosphate rock by its cadmium content. Phosphate rock is rich in fluoride too, and phosphate fertilizers have raised soil fluoride. Plants take up little, so the greater concern is livestock that eat contaminated soil. Uranium-238 runs from 7 to 100 pCi/g in phosphate rock and 1 to 67 pCi/g in phosphate fertilizers. Heavy use can raise levels in soils and drainage water several-fold. Yet the added health risk from radionuclides in food is very small, less than 0.05 mSv/y. Steel slag, recycled as an amendment for its calcium, magnesium and trace elements, can carry arsenic, cadmium, chromium and nickel, though it helps immobilize lead. Mixed with biochar, steel slag makes a good amendment for immobilizing heavy metals in farm soils.

soil-fert-015.title: How fertilizer reaches rivers, lakes and wells
soil-fert-015.text: Coastal dead zones are increasing, and nitrogen-rich water draining off farmland is the primary cause of serious oxygen depletion in coastal zones, lakes and rivers. Rain and snowmelt carry nitrogen and phosphorus off fertilized land into surface water, and leaching carries them down into groundwater. In fresh water the main culprit is phosphate. It feeds algae and cyanobacteria whose decay uses up the oxygen, the process of {{ref:soil-env-020}}, and farm drainage is a major contributor. Much of the nitrogen that plants do not take up, becomes easily leached nitrate. Groundwater above 10 mg/L can cause blue baby syndrome. Even where this can be reversed, decades of careful land care may pass before natural denitrification clears the accumulated nitrate.

soil-fert-095.title: Phosphorite, the rock behind phosphate fertilizer
soil-fert-095.text: Average sedimentary rock holds under 0.2% phosphorus. Phosphorite, or phosphate rock, ranges from 4% to 20% P2O5. It is a non-detrital sedimentary rock, one not built from worn fragments of older rock, and it is rich in phosphate minerals. The phosphate is mostly fluorapatite in very fine masses, with hydroxyapatite often derived from bones and teeth. Phosphorites form mostly in shallow seas, most commonly where strong upwelling brings deep, phosphate-rich water to the coast. About 90% of the rock goes to fertilizer and animal feed supplements. For fertilizer it must be beneficiated, upgraded by washing, flotation and similar steps, to at least 28% P2O5; most marketed grades reach 30% or more. Mined rock becomes wet-process phosphoric acid. With more rock, that acid gives the triple form of {{ref:soil-fert-094}}; with ammonia, it gives ammonium phosphates. World economic reserves stood at 70 gigatonnes in 2018, but high-grade ore is declining. Beneficiated rock is also sold as an 'organic' phosphate source, and an FAO report finds that applying it directly can be more sustainable in certain soils and countries.

soil-fert-094.title: Superphosphate, the first chemical manure
soil-fert-094.text: The world's first chemical manure went into industrial production in 1842. Its inventor, met in {{ref:soil-hist-074}}, began making his patented 'super phosphate of lime' from fossil coprolites. Superphosphate is made by treating phosphate-rich material with acid. The first, in the 1840s, used bones and sulfuric acid; makers then turned to phosphate coprolites and later to phosphorite. Single superphosphate comes from phosphate rock and sulfuric acid, and a typical fertilizer grade holds 20% P2O5, though other sources give 14–18%. Triple superphosphate, mainly monocalcium phosphate, comes from rock and phosphoric acid and holds 45%. Double superphosphate mixes both. Much of its phosphate is soluble and immediately available, giving plants a quick boost, and it is cheap enough to be widely used in developing regions. In soil, though, phosphate readily binds to clays, aluminum and iron salts or organic ligands, and much of it becomes unavailable to plants. Continuous use can acidify soils, especially poorly buffered ones. Soluble phosphate, and phosphate bound to fine particles, also washes into rivers, where it is lost to farming and feeds the overgrowth of algae.

soil-fert-046.title: Peak phosphorus: will the rock run out?
soil-fert-046.text: Phosphorus for fertilizer comes from a limited resource, and a shortage of mined phosphorus would threaten food security worldwide. Peak phosphorus names that potential shortage of economically mineable phosphorus. The term arose from the limited occurrence of rock phosphate. One estimate puts the US peak in 1988 and the world peak in 1989; others place it within the next few hundred years. Two responses could stretch supplies. Phosphorus can be recovered from excreta, for example as {{ref:soil-fert-097}} from urine or from sludge treatment liquids. And using less fertilizer, as when mycorrhizal inoculants allow lower rates, helps prolong the finite reserves.

soil-fert-040.title: Phosphate-rich organic manure: compost that unlocks rock
soil-fert-040.text: Rock phosphate locks its phosphorus in insoluble tricalcium phosphate, and composting can free it. Phosphate-rich organic manure is made by co-composting very finely ground, high-grade rock phosphate: 80% finer than 54 microns and 32% ± 2% P2O5. Microbial organic acids slowly dissolve the phosphate, and the organic matter stops other ions locking it into insoluble forms. Phosphorus dissolves best between pH 5.5 and 7. Below 5.5, aluminum, iron and manganese block its release; above 7, magnesium and calcium do. An alternative to diammonium phosphate and single superphosphate, it may add phosphorus more efficiently than chemical fertilizers and feeds a second crop as well as the first. Acidic waste solids from biogas plants can be used to make it.

soil-fert-097.title: Struvite, the mineral that clogs pipes and feeds crops
soil-fert-097.text: Wastewater plants fight a mineral that scales their pipes and pumps. Struvite, magnesium ammonium phosphate (NH4MgPO4·6H2O), forms in alkaline conditions from equal molar amounts of magnesium, ammonium and phosphate. It builds up especially after anaerobic digesters release ammonium and phosphate. It dissolves readily in acid but only sparingly in neutral or alkaline water. That nuisance is also a resource. First described as a fertilizer in 1857, struvite supplies phosphorus, nitrogen and magnesium. It can be made from urine by raising the pH and adding magnesium, and recovering phosphorus from manure and municipal wastewater as struvite appears promising.

reviews.fertilizers-manures-and-amendments: This chapter followed what people add to soil, from crushed battlefield bones and marl pits to factory ammonia and acid-treated phosphate rock. Some materials feed plants directly, like urea, UAN and superphosphate; others, like compost, mulch, lime and biochar, change the soil itself, its pH, structure, water and carbon. Each gain carries a cost to manage: nitrogen lost to the air as ammonia, phosphate feeding algae in rivers and lakes, cadmium and uranium in phosphate rock, pathogens and drug residues in manure. Coatings, inhibitors, careful timing and the multiple barrier approach all aim to keep nutrients in the soil and hazards out of the food chain. And as the best phosphate ore declines, urine, struvite, biosolids and digestate offer a way to close the loop between what people waste and what crops need.
